articles.title: Dogmatic Nordic liberals v eastern family values: culture-clash drama Fjord touches nerves in Norway and Romania
articles.summary: Cristian Mungiu’s Cannes winner echoes the news story of a Romanian couple whose children were taken by the Norwegian government. As it heads to London film festival, two writers explain how the film exposes real hypocrisies.
body: When Cristian Mungiu’s Fjord was shown in Romania as a one-day preview this June, the reception was extraordinary. Across 53 towns and 96 cinemas, the film reportedly pulled in over 40,000 viewers in a single night, a number arthouse cinema rarely sees in Romania. But the response here had little to do with cinema. It felt instead like a reopening of a familiar fault line about the clash of values within the EU itself.

The film echoes events from 2015, when the five children of Marius and Ruth Bodnariu, a Pentecostal couple from Romania living in Norway – part of a Neo-Protestant minority long viewed with suspicion in Orthodox Romania – were removed from their home by Barnevernet, Norway’s child welfare authority, amid concerns over possible corporal punishment and religious indoctrination.

The fallout in Romania stretched on for months, with diplomatic friction, public demonstrations and constant media coverage. The children were eventually returned, and the Bodnarius later resettled in Romania. Mungiu doesn’t retell the story beat for beat, but Romanian viewers had no trouble recognising where it came from.
points: Cristian Mungiu’s Cannes winner echoes the news story of a Romanian couple whose children were taken by the Norwegian government.
As it heads to London film festival, two writers explain how the film exposes real hypocrisies.

articles.title: Jonathan Glazer says Israel’s retaliation over NAZA ‘more venal’ than anticipated
articles.summary: Film’s executive producer says he was ‘shocked into silence’ the first time he watched documentary that details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza. The director Jonathan Glazer has called Israel’s retaliation against NAZA’s film-makers and the military figures interviewed in the…
body: Since the film’s release, the Israeli government has denounced it and pursued those involved, announcing plans aimed at stripping citizenship from people who “smear” Israeli soldiers; accused NAZA’s co-directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, of treason; and ordered top legal and security officials to find and prosecute soldiers and officers interviewed in the documentary for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.

Speaking to the Guardian’s editor-in-chief, Katharine Viner, at NAZA’s UK premiere in London on Thursday night, Glazer, who is an executive producer on the film, said he was “shocked into silence” the first time he watched NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza.

He noted that it was “clearly in dialogue” with and “deals with very similar themes” to The Zone of Interest, the 2023 historical drama he directed and that depicted the mundane daily lives of Nazi officers overseeing the extermination of Jews at Auschwitz.

articles.title: Busan Takeaways: Record Crowds Meet a Political Storm as Asia’s Producers Close Ranks
articles.summary: The Busan International Film Festival drew its largest film audience in more than a decade at its 31st edition, which ran Oct. 6–15, while a political firestorm over a Korean box office hit and an Iranian director’s war speech kept politics in the spotlight.
body: The 31st edition drew its biggest audiences since 2015 while the row over ‘The Assassin(s)’ and Majid Majidi’s war speech put politics center stage.
These are Variety ’s takeaways from the festival and its Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM).

Community BIFF, the audience-programmed strand in Nampo-dong, pulled in 29,511 visitors, more than 1.7 times last year’s figure. BIFF Everywhere took films to a record 18 locations, among them Buddhist temples, traditional markets and a National Assembly building in Seoul.

The ACFM, which ran Oct. 10–13 at BEXCO under the theme “Core and Expansion,” counted 30,484 visitors, up 1.6%. Registrations climbed 4.3% to 3,158 participants from 1,266 companies in 58 countries. Exhibitors rose 17% to 339 companies, 49 of them first-timers, and Czech & Slovak and Cambodian pavilions made their debuts.

articles.title: Calling the shots: what NAZA says about perpetrator cinema
articles.summary: The documentary detailing Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza is the latest film to give a voice to those who carry out atrocities – confronting viewers with some of the most difficult questions of all. Are we still talking about the banality of evil?
body: The work of directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor is shattering. But we have been shattered before by the firsthand accounts of people who carry out atrocities – sometimes called perpetrator cinema. In 2013, director Joshua Oppenheimer released The Act of Killing, an astonishing film involving members of 1960s right-wing Indonesian death squads. It was lavishly acclaimed. Since then, it has only kept feeling painfully relevant.

Questions gnaw through them all. To begin: who is it that commits crimes against humanity? The answer can feel inconclusive. NAZA is filled with Tel Aviv high-fliers, some citing as justification the horrific attacks of October 7. But the American troops of Standard Operating Procedure are ordinary grunts in the “war on terror”. Meanwhile, in The Act of Killing, ageing street thugs recreate their murders of trade unionists and teachers as the action movies they imagine them being. Flamboyance blooms in the abyss.
points: Are we still talking about the banality of evil?

articles.title: Serielizados Program: Steven Moffat, Ferran Adrià, and Rodrigo Sorogoyen Bring Star Creator Power to Barcelona
articles.summary: Carmen Machi, Rodrigo Sorogoyen, Hagai Levi, Steven Moffat, Sue Vertue, Victoria Martín, Ferran Adrià. All will bring star power to Barcelona’s leading series festival Serielizados which is set to kick-off Oct.
body: You said last year that your goal was both to up your number of visitors and to better serve the local industry. Is it mission accomplished after last year’s 80% increase in visitors and Serielizados Pro’s first Mind the Gap?

Yes, we totally accomplished that and after growing by 80% last year, our challenge this edition is consolidation. Our main hurdle has always been convincing people to pay for a cinema ticket to watch two episodes of a series. We’ve overcome that by not only premiering great series but also bringing the talent directly to the fans.

On the industry side, Serielizados Pro has settled into its identity as a boutique forum. We don’t want to be huge; we want to be effective. We focus heavily on European co-productions, matching local Catalan and Spanish creators with international agents through pitching sessions, masterclasses, and networking.
In fact, after our first Mind the Gap Pitching, we’re already seeing participating projects secure financing and move into production, which proves that the concept works.

articles.title: ‘Avatar: Fire and Ash’ Composer and More Speak Out About AI at Ghent’s WSA Film Music Days: ‘We Must Continue to Defend Our Art’
articles.summary: At a recent World Soundtrack Awards industry panel, composer Simon Franglen struck a common chord when talking about his work on “Avatar: Fire and Ash.” “We had hundreds of musicians in a room, pouring their emotion out in that precise second,” he recalled.
body: Labor structures are a hurdle. Unlike many other key creatives and department heads, composers in the U.S. and U.K. face legal barriers to unionizing and collective bargaining. The European Composer and Songwriter Alliance helps fill that gap, uniting national associations to lobby policymakers and guide young composers through contracts and negotiations.
Representing more than 30,000 composers and songwriters across 57 member organizations, ECSA had a strong presence in Ghent, hosting a roundtable before receiving this year’s WSA Industry Award.

“There’s still a long way to go and a lot of work to do,” ECSA president Helienne Lindvall said in accepting the award. “But one thing is clear: We have become a voice to be reckoned with, giving composers and songwriters a seat at the table. Because, as someone once said, if you’re not sitting at the table, chances are you’re on the menu.”

articles.title: 'People call them pervert glasses': Blind users fear backlash over smart tech
articles.summary: Concerns about the use of smart glasses are having an affect on visually-impaired users.
body: Fraser Fleming approaches the corner of a busy Glasgow city centre street and asks his smart glasses to describe the road ahead.
A voice coming from tiny speakers in the arms of the specs tells him there are several parked cars and a person walking in his direction.
For 44-year-old Fraser, who is registered blind, this is "game changing" information.
"I know how to approach the street and what sort of care to take," he says.

articles.title: Porn showing choking or incest to be banned from early November, government says
articles.summary: The move follows a review into pornography regulation in 2025 by Conservative peer Baroness Gabby Bertin
body: Online pornography depicting strangulation or incestuous relationships will be banned from early November, the government has announced.

From 6 November, it will be illegal to possess or publish porn which shows strangulation or suffocation, depicts sexual activity between people who are related or shows adults role-playing as children under 16.
The new rules follow a review into porn regulation in 2025 which found depictions of choking were "rife" on popular porn sites and had helped normalise the act among young people.
Conservative peer Baroness Gabby Bertin, who headed the review, said the news came "not a moment too soon".

articles.title: ‘Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald’ Review: Judd Apatow’s Latest Comedy Doc Sends Viewers Down a Laugh-Filled Rabbit Hole
articles.summary: The Netflix film skips traditional talking heads for a more archival approach to the 'Saturday Night Live' and 'Dirty Work' comedy legend.
body: As much as I adore Freaks and Geeks and Undeclared and The 40-Year-Old Virgin and Knocked Up, it’s becoming increasingly clear that Judd Apatow ‘s greatest legacy may be the documentary project he started fairly late in his career.

Hitting Netflix one week ahead of Apatow and Neil Berkeley’s Paralyzed by Hope: The Maria Bamford Story (and one week after the Berkeley-co-directed documentary about Marin Mull), Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald finds Apatow continuing to experiment formally.

If Mel Brooks: The 99 Year Old Man! was driven by the remarkable gift of Brooks’ ongoing presence in our cultural lives and The Zen Diaries of Garry Shandling was driven by Shandling’s unreleased diaries, Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald defies the notion of documentary as a path toward intimacy. This is the first of the Apatow docs that feels more like an opportunity to point and laugh at favorite one-liners and late-night appearances than to learn anything deeper and more personal about its subject, which is simultaneously a limitation and the purpose here.
points: The Netflix film skips traditional talking heads for a more archival approach to the 'Saturday Night Live' and 'Dirty Work' comedy legend.
